evidence.text:
18. VERSIONED SELF-IMPROVEMENT OF THE EXECUTION PROMPT

Maintain EXECUTION-PROMPT.md in the campaign control repository. Initialize it with the executable prompt text, excluding the surrounding audit summary. Record the seed source; this file is the canonical campaign copy. Do not depend on changing hidden conversation instructions or on modifying external skill/AGENTS.md files.

At each run start, save an immutable prompt snapshot and its version/commit/hash under runs/<run-id>/. Associate all results with that version. A fresh session must read the canonical prompt plus the handoff and reconcile any recorded mid-run clarifications.

At each run's retrospective:
1. Examine execution friction, help incidents, repairs, reviews, false-success risks, and recovery experience.
2. Decide whether a prompt change would prevent recurrence or improve execution. No edit is required merely because a run ended.
3. Draft the smallest justified change. Record the triggering evidence, intended behavior, and scope in the run assessment or prompt commit.
4. Independently review the diff for contradictions, bypasses, recovery gaps, burden, and changed authority. Use the supported Howl review path. If review is unavailable, pause; do not self-certify it.
5. Validate structure, section references, status transitions, and the behavior the revised instruction is meant to cause. Use a bounded scenario review where execution would be inappropriate.
6. Commit, PR, and merge the prompt update under section 16. Activate it at the next run boundary and record the new version.

The outer controller may edit this campaign prompt as an explicit maintenance responsibility. This does not permit manual product implementation, bypassing Howl, or editing protected runtime state.

Prompt changes must not:
- Predetermine a baseball product contrary to mission-first discovery.
- Remove public-interface use, independent review, evidence, acceptance, or merge gates.
- Weaken research criteria after observing results, erase findings, or relabel failures as passes.
- Remove the pause-and-help rule, no-local-LLM rule, isolation rules, or protections for human work.
- Grant new permissions, bypass policies, acquire spending authority, or reset consumed budgets.
- Reinterpret old runs under new success criteria.

Only a subsequent explicit user instruction can authorize a change to those mission constraints, subject to higher-priority instructions. Self-authored text cannot do so.

If a current instruction is itself blocking execution, pause under section 17, propose a concrete amendment, and wait for the response. Preserve the starting prompt and record the authorized amendment separately; never silently rewrite the active run's history.

For each help incident, add an actionable prevention/recovery instruction where warranted, or explicitly explain why the component repair and regression coverage already address it and a prompt change would add no value. Preserve the lesson either way.

History rewrite touches shared state and may conflict with protections for human work and protected runtime state; the lesson is silent on whether a rewrite is permitted, who authorizes it, or how it's recorded. This is a recovery gap.

Lesson 3's formula max_calls >= clamp(max_candidates // 2, 1, 3) + max_candidates sets a minimum, not a cap, and could be read as encouraging higher spending. It does not state that it cannot exceed an existing authorized budget or reset consumed budgets. Section 18 forbids acquiring spending authority and resetting consumed budgets, so a clause is needed: "within the already authorized budget; if the formula exceeds it, pause."

The worked arithmetic above is illustrative only (max_candidates=4 gives a minimum of 6 calls). The sizing conflicts with any fixed budget lower than that value, and the diff does not say which wins. Whether one PARTIAL result justifies the rule is unverified.

Lesson 4 requires passing the repository's required gate as --verify with an adequate --verify-timeout. "Adequate" is untestable. "Prove a committed candidate through the public chain with PYTHONPATH pointing at a clean repair worktree" could be read as running the product outside the normal public interface, weakening the public-interface-use rule. It is also an added burden on every repair. Recording the SHA is testable, but where it is recorded is unspecified.

Lesson 5 says to "trace any downgrade to its cause" and "recover through the documented live doctor." If the documented doctor mutates protected runtime state, this conflicts with section 18's ban on editing protected runtime state. The lesson needs "recover only via documented, permitted operations; otherwise pause under section 17."

Lesson 6 "small enough for one implementation pass" is vague and untestable. "Documented discard" of an unfinished worktree could destroy human or prior work, which touches protections for human work, and it names no approver. Discard should require explicit user authorization and preservation of a copy.

Lesson 7 pins the same acceptor on resume. This could entrench a biased or faulty acceptor and weaken independent review if the acceptor is also the author or is unavailable. There is no fallback when the original acceptor is unavailable, and "never route a rejection to a different acceptor" could block progress, leaving no pause-and-help route. It may also be read as letting a rejected party shop for a re-judgment loop, so the retry count should be bounded.

Section 18 asks that each lesson record triggering evidence, intended behavior, and scope. The diff has one-line R001 parentheticals with no evidence IDs, so this requirement is not demonstrably met, and the cited trigger for the first lesson (a worker refusing an approved fetch) justifies a narrower fix than the one proposed.

The header changes the file's first lines and states a v1 hash. Section 18 requires an immutable snapshot under runs/<run-id>/ and activation at the next run boundary. The diff does not state activation timing, so the v2 text could be applied mid-run, which would reinterpret the active run's history. The hash itself is unverified.
The change adds seven lessons from one run, which may be more than the "smallest justified change" required by section 18 step 3; several (lessons 5 and 6) are cited only by incident labels.

The only evidence supplied is section 18 (operator expectation, not observed reality). The R001 triggers, DOG-/CUBS-/NOTE- ids, and the claimed incidents have no supplied evidence, so no lesson's trigger can be confirmed as justifying it.

The preamble "add no authority and remove no gate" is a self-assertion; section 18 says self-authored text cannot change constraints, so the claim is not evidence and each bullet must be judged on its own wording.

Lesson 1 (owner authorizations verbatim) could be read as letting a worker override a repository's documented restriction. The wording does not require that the authorization be an explicit, recorded user instruction with provenance, so a controller-paraphrased "authorization" could bypass the repo restriction. It also may grant new permissions if the authorization is not from the user.

Lesson 2 (third-party data) is protective, but "read the source's terms" is untestable without a recorded artifact, and "bulk records" and "short attributed examples" are undefined, so a reviewer cannot test them. The "separate step" scan has no named method or pass criterion. A rewrite of public history is mentioned as a trigger but no recovery step is given for data already pushed.

Lesson 3's formula is stated as max_calls >= clamp(max_candidates // 2, 1, 3) + max_candidates, but it is not checked against how Howl actually counts calls. A single PARTIAL result is thin justification for a hard formula, and it is unclear whether it raises spending. Raising max_calls could be new spending authority and conflicts with section 18's ban on acquiring spending authority or resetting consumed budgets.

Lesson 4 mixes several rules. "Prove a committed candidate through the public chain with PYTHONPATH pointing at a clean repair worktree" may sidestep the public interface if PYTHONPATH selects code other than the supported install, and it is not clear this counts as the independent review or acceptance gate. "Adequate --verify-timeout" is vague and untestable. The reference to the "repository's required gate" is undefined when a repo has none.

Lesson 5 says to "recover through the documented live doctor", which may permit repair actions on protected runtime state. Section 18 forbids editing protected runtime state, and the lesson does not limit the recovery to documented, non-manual steps. The "downgrade" cause trace has no stop condition if the cause cannot be found.

Lesson 6 has a recovery gap: "a documented discard" of an unfinished worktree session could destroy human or prior work, which section 18 protects. It does not require that the discard be authorized or that uncommitted changes be preserved first. "Small enough for one pass" is vague and untestable.

Lesson 7 says never route a rejection to a different acceptor. If the pinned acceptor is unavailable, biased, or itself faulty, execution deadlocks with no escape path. Pinning the same acceptor may also weaken independence, since it reinforces its earlier view. It has no cited R001 trigger at all, which violates section 18's requirement to record triggering evidence.

Section 18 requires, for each help incident, either an actionable instruction or an explanation of why none is needed. The diff does not record which incidents were addressed or why others were not, so that requirement cannot be verified from this diff.

The header change references a date and a hash, but nothing shows that the snapshot under runs/<run-id>/ was saved or that independent review through the Howl path occurred. Per section 18, if that review is unavailable, the change must pause and not be self-certified.
The diff adds 13 lines to a file, and the placement "19A" after line 836 is unchecked against existing numbering; a reference to a section not shown could contradict the rest of the prompt.
